annotation.text: Good evening, everyone.
My name is Leslie Cormack, and I am the Dean of the Faculty of Arts here at the University
of Alberta, and I'm delighted to welcome you to this, the 11th Annual Henry Kreisel Honorary
Lecture.
I want to begin by respectfully acknowledging that the University of Alberta is located
on Treaty 6 territory, the traditional lands of First Nations and Métis people.
And then I want to welcome you to this wonderful event hosted by the Canadian Literature Centre.
Because my mother went to the University of Alberta here in the 1940s, she was taught
by Henry Kreisel, and so this lecture has always had a very important part in my heart
as I think about the history of this great university.
This event has become a flagship event for the Canadian Literature Centre, which offers
many activities and speakers to the community, to communities really, throughout the year.
I'm very proud of the fact that the Canadian Literature Centre is part of the Faculty of
Arts, and I've been delighted to see it grow over the years.
It has grown tremendously in the years that it has existed, and is now firmly established,
I think, nationally and internationally as a leading force in the support of Canadian
literatures and cultures.
The Faculty of Arts is committed to the support of the diversity and outstanding vitality
of Canadian literature, as exemplified in the work that the CLC does each and every
day, and exemplified even more in this year's guest lecturer.
I want to thank Eric and Alexis Schloss, as well as Jim and Betty Edwards, for their generous
founding gifts and their continued support of the Canadian Literature Centre.
I also want to thank all the other donors, whether you're here in the room or in absentia,
who work to make the work of the CLC possible.
And of course, I especially right now want to thank the people at the CLC who organized
today's event, Dr. Daniel Laforet, Acting Director of the CLC, and his team, Jason Purcell
and Anna Chodacky.
And now I'd like to call on Dr. Laforet to offer a few words.
Thank you very much.
Good evening.
Bonsoir.
Dr. Eric Schloss, distinguished guests, esteemed members of the Inmonton public, all of you
literature lovers without the support of which none of this would be possible.
I am Daniel Laforet, Acting Director of the CLC for the winter and the spring, and I'm
very pleased to welcome you to the 11th installment of the CLC Kreisel Lecture.
The lecture series was founded in 2007 to honour the memory of a foremost Canadian intellectual,
the author, university professor, and officer of the Order of Canada, Henry Kreisel.
He inspired generations of students to love literature and was one of the first people
to incorporate the immigrant experience to modern Canadian literature.
Since its inception, the Kreisel Lecture Series has become the flagship event of the CLC.
Throughout the years, we've had the chance to hear some of the nation's most eloquent
and popular voices, Lawrence Hill, Izzy Edugyan, Annabelle Lyon, Danila Ferriere, Margaret Atwood,
among others.
Our evening with Heather O'Neill tonight will be no exception, trust me.
Sitting here together tonight, we're all taking part in a lively, vibrant tradition, and I
want to thank you all for it.
So before I leave the stage, there are a couple of things that you need to know.
Every Kreisel Lecture is an original text by the guest author, and they are all published
by University of Alberta Press.
Last year's lecture by Margaret Atwood just came out.
You will be able to purchase...
Well, you're already able to purchase it on the bookselling table provided by Audrey's
Books down and during the reception afterwards, down there.
Tonight's lecture by Heather O'Neill will also be available in the same published format
next year.
Second thing I want you to know is for those who are inclined to do so, we encourage live
tweeting tonight.
The hashtag is Kreisel2017, so that's K-R-E-I-S-E-L, 2017 in one word, without space.
Now to offer a more formal and engaging introduction to Heather O'Neill's talk tonight, I'm pleased
to welcome on stage my colleague from Montreal University in Calgary, non-fiction author
and Canadian scholar extraordinaire, Mr. Kit Dobson.
Thank you, Kit.
Welcome to the 2017 Henry Kreisel Commemorative Lecture.
Thank you for being here tonight at this fantastic Tim's Centre for the Arts at the University
of Alberta.
So my name is Kit Dobson, I'm a faculty member in English at Montreal University in Calgary.
Thank you so much to the Canadian Literature Centre, especially Daniel Laforet, Marie Carrière,
Jason, Anna, and the folks who make this place work.
It is an honour to be here and to have the privilege to introduce you to our guest speaker.
When I was asked to introduce Heather O'Neill, I felt very lucky and fortunate, yet also
challenged.
Heather O'Neill is, on the one hand, someone who can be introduced based on her achievements.
Born, raised, and resident of Montreal, she is the author of three jaw-droppingly good
novels, Lullabies for Little Criminals, The Girl Who Was Saturday Night, and her new novel,
2017's The Lonely Heart's Hotel, as well as a short story collection, Daydreams of Angels,
and the collection of poems, Two Eyes, Are You Sleeping?
Her work has won Canada Reads, the Hugh MacLennan Award, the Danuta Glead Award, and she has
been on the list for many of the top national and international literary prizes, like the
Giller Prize, the Governor General's Award, and the Impact Dublin Literary Award.
The accolades are mounting and, I will wager, are only going to continue with the publication
of her new work.
But an introduction of this sort sells Heather's achievements short, at least in my view.
Heather O'Neill's writing is difficult, challenging, yet beautiful and soothing.
The focus on her novels, in particular, might allow us to see a little bit of what I mean.
Her first novel, Lullabies for Little Criminals, published in 2006, features Baby, a girl who
lives in central Montreal.
She spends her time wandering through the plateau, her eyes full of the wonder and curiosity
that can characterize young people just coming into themselves.
She is remarkably open to the world, fantastically perceptive, and as troublesome as can be.
The world of wonders in which Baby lives, however, is a frightening one to read from
this side of adolescence.
We watch her father's battle with his addiction continue to worsen and, as no one maintains
much interest in guiding Baby, the neighbourhood pimp begins to take an interest.
Throughout Lullabies for Little Criminals, Heather presents us with a doubled vision,
that which Baby manages somehow to maintain, one that hangs on to childhood despite terrible
circumstances.
The other vision is that which the reader brings to the text, one that is full of concern
for the wayward protagonist and wary of each of her troubling decisions.
Heather's subsequent novel, The Girl Who Was Saturday Night, published in 2014, returns
us to the plateau in Montreal, this time to the era of the second referendum in Quebec.
Her protagonist, Nushka, and her protagonist's brother, Nicholas, are the children of a once-famous,
now failed and disgraced fictional singer associated with the Quebecois nationalist
movement.
Nushka and Nicholas experience young lives of rash acts.
They discover sex through their lives in the neighbourhood, and they struggle to survive
in their impoverished surroundings.
At the same time as their lives are unfolding, a documentary film crew descends upon them,
seeking to make a film about their dysfunctional family.
Here again, the plateau, and the Boulevard Saint-Laurent in particular, is a site of
unusual assortments, of people who hang around, smoking their cigarettes in impossible weather,
and who offer Nushka and Nicholas worrying openings to adulthood.
The novel is brimful of a feeling of wasted decadence, of risk, and of cats.
O'Neill's writing is always, it seems, full of cats, and of characters, who are tragically
flawed, yet who are nonetheless honest and true.
Her new novel also begins with Montreal, but the historical Montreal of the Depression.
It stars the orphaned children, Rose and Pierrot, who, after being raised in the same orphanage,
struggle to find their way in Montreal's underworld, a place populated by gangsters.
Their mistresses, sex workers, addicts, and clowns.
As in her previous work, Heather's writing is difficult and challenging, yet beautiful
and soothing.
Rose and Pierrot manage to retain their whimsy and their charm, despite a world that would
harden them, that would harm them, and that would, at times, eliminate them entirely.
The turn in this recent novel, this new novel, to a more historical focus, is something that
interests me greatly, but I am, above all else, deeply compelled by her characters.
For it is her characters, above all, who are difficult, challenging, beautiful, and
soothing.
This combination is not an easy one to maintain.
I find that reading Heather's work is like eating ice cream on a hot summer's day.
Even if you don't want to do so, even if you wish to savour it, you have to rush, you have
to go at it with gusto and abandon, lest it melt all over you.
Her books read like melting ice cream.
If that simile seems a bit laboured, and it probably is, that's in part because my own
similes simply cannot keep up with Heather's.
Heather O'Neill is, in my view, also the finest writer of the simile in contemporary literature.
Similes leap from her pages, and I find myself anticipating the next like or as comparison.
Many of her paragraphs build up to outrageously perfect ones.
I had so many to choose from, but I will limit myself to one such example, since we are here
to hear from her.
Early on in her new novel, we read the following, quote, "'Rose' and Pierrot were orphans.
There was something magical about hearing them talk about their tragic circumstances
in such high-pitched voices.
They were metaphors for sadness.
It was like someone playing a requiem on a xylophone.
It wasn't something you heard every day," end of that quotation.
Like someone playing a requiem on a xylophone, it's a perfect simile, but it's one that needs
everything that comes before it.
It needs the sweep of the narrative and of the metaphor to bring into relief the dissonant
contrast between the form of the requiem and the utterly inadequate instrument of the xylophone.
The clash is both funny and sad."
Again and again, her paragraphs soar to the point of the simile, to the moment where everything
is revealed through a comparison that forces readers to pause and to recognize precisely
what a driving force is at work in this writing.
For these reasons and more, I find myself thinking about Heather's writing in my own
modest endeavors.
Last year, I had the tremendous privilege to live in Montreal, in the heart of the plateau
that Heather's work manages to describe so beautifully.
I was there in part to write about that city.
With my children and my partner, we spent our time gathering fragments of whimsy, which
we found in every direction we turned.
Learning the meaning of the word whimsy, in fact, was a very important part of our conversations
with our two daughters.
We watched acrobats practicing in the park.
We saw unicyclists pushing forward into blizzards.
We said hello to cats walking across fence tops.
And we noticed a steady stream of university students in oversized sunglasses eating ice
cream on the street corners.
Every weekend brought a new festival, and the street art was as fantastic as the galleries,
even if the roads were sometimes impassable.
It is a city that Heather's writing captures magnificently, and that I enjoyed all the
more for reading her works while I was there.
As I cede the floor now to Heather O'Neill, I think that it is worth noticing a small,
but perhaps important, coincidence.
This year, as we've already heard, marks the 11th Kreisel Commemorative Lecture.
The number 11 seems to be a magical number in the Lonely Hearts Hotel, popping up at
important junctures.
The number 11 serves as a code between Rose and Pierrot.
It is their default number, and it is the age at which they both agree that they were
the happiest.
Perhaps this time, this 11th occasion of this lecture, may be among our happiest too.
Folks, it's my pleasure to introduce Heather O'Neill.
Hi, thank you all for coming.
I was born in Montreal and spent my first years in the city.
When I was five, my parents got divorced.
My mom packed me up and put me in the backseat of our burgundy car.
She tossed my dad's stuff out of the trunk, and we drove down to Virginia, where she was
from.
After two and a half years of moving around, she told me she had changed her mind about
wanting to be my mother.
She basically broke up with me.
She put me on a plane, and I showed up back in Montreal, where I was to spend the rest
of my childhood with my father.
A bit about my father.
My dad was a petty criminal as a child.
He worked sneaking into windows for older, hardened criminals.
He was in prison when he was 11 years old.
As an adult, he worked as a janitor, but he saw himself as street smart.
He had a little silver transistor radio that he attached to his belt.
This kept him abreast of the news.
He listened to it so often that he assumed he wasn't as intelligent as the most intelligent
people were.
My dad was determined to take care of me properly.
He made me pancakes and cookies and sewed my clothes properly.
He was actually really good at that.
What he was a little worse at was what he regarded as an integral part of parenting,
the dispensing of life advice.
But nonetheless, it was one of his favorite things to do.
He liked spending time with me because I had to look up to him.
I was only seven.
He treated me as though I was his junior partner.
He had several rules he was adamant about.
One, never keep a diary.
The other thing was that I...
I couldn't not keep a diary. I had been given a journal when I was eight years old by an
uncle. I loved the feeling of chronicling my daily events in the black journal. I quite
liked books of all types, but here was a book that had empty pages. It was waiting for me
to put words down on it. It made the events of the day seem important and worthy of a
novel. But my dad was insistent I knock it off. He told me it was a terrible habit because
everything that one wrote in a diary was ultimately used against a person in court. He's seen
to think this was an inevitable life event. But I wonder whether he felt exposed. I wonder
if he felt as though he were under surveillance, as though I would be able to return to these
as an adult and then judge what he had done in his behavior rather than my own. For as
a child, I was always innocent. But no matter how many journals he threw out, I would continue
to write in them. I'm writing in one now. He was also always redacting my letters to
my grandmother, wiping out lines with a big black marker and then making me rewrite it
at the end. Lesson number two, learn to play the tuba. My dad was insistent that when I
got to high school, I play the tuba. My dad said the world didn't have enough tuba players,
so there would always be a shortage of them. And you could always get a job if you played
the tuba. I was very worried about being able to earn a living. So if I was just allowed
to play the tuba in music class, my problems would already be over when I was 11. There
were girls in my class that told me I was too skinny to play the tuba and that it was
always given to the fattest kid. But I was sure that I could hold it. I thought that
it would be like having a baby elephant in my lap all the time, and that seemed like
such a good thing. I looked at the tuba with such longing and desire as though it were
a fat millionaire in a tailored suit who could have taken care of me for the rest of my life.
But there was only one tuba, and it was given to a really big boy. Instead, I was given
a trumpet. I always wept playing the trumpet for the first three months. The teacher said
that there was a peculiar sadness to the way I played. I earned an A in music class, although
I never believed I deserved it.
Lesson number three, make friends with Jewish kids. Another of my dad's commandments was
that I hang out and pay attention to what the Jewish kids were up to. He grew up in
a working-class neighborhood that was filled with French Canadians and Jewish kids. The
Jews had lived in apartments next to him. They had come out to play with him in their
pea caps and dirty undershirts. They had swam in the river and cursed and laughed together.
The Jewish kids all went to high school and university. They had all left the neighborhood
and did interesting things with themselves. The Jews who had grown up during the Depression
in Montreal were a marvelous and magically upwardly mobile class. While the Jewish kids
he grew up with were now running their own companies and factories, he was pretty much
where he started off. They had somehow got ahead of him, so he was adamant that I always
do what the Jewish kids were doing. They were on their way to great places.
I had a very good friend named Malachi when I was nine. He wore Adidas shorts and gym
socks up to his knees. He brought a walkie-talkie and would stay up late chatting with truck
drivers. They would have a lot of time on their hands. He was saving all his paper route
money because he wanted to go to therapy. He quite liked the idea of it. He asked his
parents and they said no way, they weren't paying for it because there was nothing wrong
with him. We spent a lot of time sitting at the bottom of the swimming pool wearing goggles
and looking at each other. I'm not exactly sure what I learned about success from hanging
out with my Jewish friends, but they were some of the most wonderful pals I ever had.
Lesson four, accept that you're ugly and move on. My dad said when I was a baby I was so
ugly that he was afraid to look at me. He would close his eyes and say, no, she couldn't
have been that ugly. But then when he opened them again, there I was, even uglier than
he remembered. He said my eyes looked like they were jumping out of my skull. He was
so embarrassed at the hospital when I was born, when he rode the bus home with me in
his arms, he put a blanket over my head so as not to shock the other passengers.
He said that when I cried as a child, the most frightening howl came out of my mouth.
Once there was an alley cat on the fire escape trying to get in the window, having mistaken
me for one of its own. He had to throw a glass of water at it to make it leave. Sometimes
I like to imagine that cat with a paw filled with flowers and bow tie on its neck knocking
on the window looking for me. As a child, he also told me he was afraid to open the
window because a wind would blow in and pick me up and carry me away because my ears were
so large. He told me once I really didn't need to take the school bus. All I had to
do was hold my hair in a ponytail and I could use my ears to fly to school like Dumbo.
He called me chicken legs as an affectionate nickname because he said I was so skinny.
I grew up thinking I was butt ugly, but it was kind of nice thinking I was ugly. It made
me feel I had to work on other attributes. It took the pressure off of ever even bothering
to try to look good. Otherwise, little girls are bombarded with praise for superficial
qualities informed from the time they can understand a sentence what the male gaze thinks
of them. I liked the idea of being unique and if I could be the ugliest baby in the
whole city, that seemed like an accomplishment. Number five, never tell anyone what you do
for a living. My father told me I should never tell anyone what my parents did for a living
for God's sakes. He said it was no one's business to begin with and he said they would
judge me and never give me any opportunities in life. On my birth registry under occupation,
my father wrote that he was a professor of philosophy. Now, my father dropped out of
school in grade three and his reading skills were rather limited. He always got me to read
everything that came in the mail out loud to him, so it might seem an outrageous lie
to claim he was a professor of philosophy, but the lie to me wasn't completely out of
left field. He did tend to pontificate and his friends did listen to what he said and
contemplate his conclusions and assumptions. I think that lying is just a way of telling
the truth in a metaphorical way. In elementary school, I always had to fill out the form
with parental information. He told me to tell the teacher he was a spy and therefore all
the required information was classified. The gym teacher asked me if it was true that my
father was a spy. I looked down at my burgundy Adidas running shoes and gave my rote response,
I'm not at liberty to say. When I enrolled in high school, he listed his profession as
sculptor. Well, that year he had a job as a janitor for a building and the fence around
the building came down, so he'd been collecting broken hockey sticks outside the skating rink
for years. He sawed off the blades of hockey sticks and drilled them together and made
this very strange fence out of them. Everyone stopped and stared at his construction. He
had probably lowered the property value by about $100,000 in one morning, but occasionally
one of the viewers would exclaim that this was quite marvelous, a true objet d'art. By
teaching me to lie about who I was, my dad instilled in me the notion that the differences
were actually superficial. They were all just outward trappings and if you were to change
coats with a rich person, then you would immediately be one. In life, there will always be someone
trying to take your personhood away. They're trying to get you to think you are less than
you are. It happens with color, gender, class, education. There are people who will have
you believe that class is genetic and that you are less of a person than them. I was
a child of a janitor, but he wanted me to be treated like the child of a professor of
philosophy. Lesson six, know something about history. My dad was a hoarder. He always came
home with objects he had found in the garbage in his pockets. There's a certain relationship
that poor people have to their objects and things, a tenderness. Because they have nothing
of value, they bequeath the value onto plain objects and this in turn makes them cherished.
It's not the object, but what it symbolizes, what it was supposed to be. Let me elaborate.
My dad would give everything he brought home a backstory. According to him, he had traveled
all of Europe during the Second World War to get many of the objects in our apartment.
There was a dessert spoon he said he had bought from a witch in Bulgaria. There was a tray
for cookies that had come from Poland from a woman who had one eye who wore compression
gym socks and had an adult child who suffered from ulcers and couldn't work and had to live
off of selling magical cookies. He told me he had learned to make pork chops in a five
star restaurant in Paris. He was a top chef there and would have to make seven dishes
at once. There were escargot climbing all over the walls and sometimes sad frogs in
glass jars. He once set a frog free by flushing it down the toilet and wishing it Godspeed.
I never knew whether I believed this or not and it seemed irrelevant whether it was true.
I liked listening to the stories. He never let anything be ordinary. Everything around
me from the doorknob to the lamp was splendid with meaning and belonged to a museum. I guess
I got a sense of the history of the modern world through these stories, albeit a racist,
stereotypical and ethnocentric one, but still. Once I was walking to school and I passed
a quilt in the garbage. When I came home later in that day, the same quilt had been washed
in iron and folded at the foot of my bed. He told me he had paid good money for it at
an auction in old Montreal. I have a shelf with absurd objects that my dad gave me as
gifts. My friends will often stop in front of it. They will say something to the nature
of, the hell is this shelf of worthless tacky junk? At which point I will often explain
the origins of these articles, how each one was given to me by my father when he would
come to visit. Then they will think of them as beautiful. The ceramic goose with the top
hat will suddenly seem debonair and begin to tell a tale about its childhood outside
Berlin. Lesson number seven. No matter what anyone tells you, crime certainly pays.
When he was young, my dad had been a great criminal. He was very proud of these years.
Not having pursued a life of crime had been the great regret of his life, I think. He
wanted to have been a gangster that Martin Scorsese made movies about. He thought their
lives were wonderful. They had escaped their class with a vengeance, exacting a reckoning
on everyone who belittled them and then everyone else just for good measure. What was there
not to love? We watched every gangster film many times. My dad believed that breaking
the law was, in certain circumstances, not a problem. He definitely had a lax view about
stealing because he did it all the time. As a child, I was crazy about cheese. So in
the evenings, my father would stop at select grocery stores to steal the most expensive
cheese on display. At home, he would arrange them on a plate covered in rabbits that was
my favorite. Blue cheese, Camembert, Gruyere. He would pronounce them in funny ways because
he couldn't really read well. He would put them on my lap while we were watching television
and we would eat them with toothpicks with really frilly ribbons on them. We'd watch
Benny Hill and turn and nod to each other whenever the mouthful was particularly delightful.
I think no one would argue with the idea that if a parent steals food for a child, then
they should not be convicted of anything at all. This is a crime driven out of necessity.
It's almost a duty to commit such a crime. However, would one argue that it is necessary
to steal one's child outrageously expensive cheese when the child has a taste for such?
My father said my taste in cheese shows I was refined. It proved I was descended somehow
from French aristocrats. He continued to steal delicacies from the supermarket for me throughout
my childhood. Caviar, m'lady, he said one night, pulling a tiny jar from his left pocket.
Ooh, I declared. From out of his other pocket, he pulled a box of tiny marzipan apples. What
could I do but applaud and throw my arms around his neck? By the end of his life, we would
have to take the city bus a mile before we could go to any grocery store that would let
him in. He had been banned from all the ones in the neighborhood. Nobody was going to put
you in jail for stealing a fancy imported bottle of olive oil for your child, but they
would bar you from ever returning. However, the takeaway from this was that I should not
settle with what was offered me in life. I should want more than what my father could
afford, and I was expected to find some other methods other than stealing to get them in
life. Lesson eight, all sophisticated people have dinner parties. My dad and I liked to
go to Warshaw's, this great family-run grocery store. They don't really have grocery stores
like that anymore. Used to be able to fall in love with the grocery store. In the back,
there were always a shelf of random items for sale, tea sets, woks, flower pots, etc.
And they were always offered at cut-throat prices. One afternoon, we chanced upon a fondue
pot. My dad helped it up. This was it. There would be no difference between us and the
millionaires now. If we were eating fondue, then we were eating like King Henry VIII.
No way around it. He bought the fondue pot, since he couldn't exactly fit it in his pocket.
For the next week, my dad began to make preparations for our fondue dinner. He decided to invite
all our loved ones over, because there's no point in going through the trouble of having
a fondue dinner without inviting loads of people to share. My dad hated his biological
family with a passion, so none of them were invited. But he called up all his friends.
My dad's friends were an eclectic bunch. He had a friend who had robbed a bank and served
11 years in prison, Matthew. Matthew had also promised to take care of his friend's handicapped
daughter after he died, and he was true to this commitment. He was very mild-mannered
and was always on his way to the grocery store to fill up on his Pepsi. He kept to his absurd
tasks all day. He taught me about how you can remake your life at any time in life,
and how true goodness came from unexpected sources. There was a rather bright man named
Sylvain who I adored. He was skinny, and he had a lovely way of speaking. He wore a suit
and would often have a flower in the boutonniere. He reminded me of people from PBS shows. He
would drink and start to laugh and weep. His moods were roller coasters. They were Shakespearean
tragedies. His flights of fancy were a primer for understanding Shakespeare and some of
the important work I did at McGill. There was a guy named Percival. He used to walk
around the city all day to calm his nerves. He walked as though it were a job. Animals
liked him, though. He would speak to our toy poodle in such high-pitched voices that it
would actually faint from joy. He could whistle like all kinds of birds. Since I lived downtown,
I didn't know what a bird other than a pigeon sounded like, but the noises he made were
quite beautiful just the same. He was a modern-day Kierkegaard. He really could have written
Fear and Trembling on the existential anxiety and the terrifying responsibility of choice.
He had another friend who came over who had managed to get him to write a book about him.
He had managed to buy a tiny house for himself years before, it had been declared an eyesore
by the city.
They'd warned him to clean it up, but he didn't want to.
He said he'd worked his whole life and now it was his prerogative to live in filth.
There would be stray cats sitting on the eaves of the house and vines trying to push the
windows open like thieves.
I think I actually learned nothing from him, but I'm still trying to figure out the lesson.
After dinner, they'd go sit on a bench on the corner, hopefully there would be a large
appliance in the garbage that they could test their respective strengths by lifting.
I would go with them and my dad would give me change to go buy a bottle of tonic water
to drink.
My dad insisted tonic water was only for Friday nights.
When I grew up, I was surprised that other people didn't find it was a treat.
But there would be no sitting on the bench that evening.
My dad somehow thought you could only eat fondue in the dark, as though it were a campfire
to scare away minuscule wolves.
Because we had to wait until the sun went down, everyone got hungry and then they started
drinking on empty stomachs.
And then they started going completely insane.
They started feeling sorry for themselves, and when men who are over 50 and have nothing
to show for it begin to feel sorry for themselves, mayhem ensues.
They all started setting their money on fire.
Then they started singing and arm wrestling and falling down the stairs.
So they ended up outside, yelling in the middle of the street that no one had ever
loved him.
Ignore him, my dad said, as I dipped the bread into the cheese.
All in all, it was a great night.
Everyone had an opportunity to pontificate and articulate their rage and concerns.
Everyone had a chance to declare that love was a sham, ex-wives were toasted sarcastically,
threats to enemies were made, religion was condemned, universal outrage was the order
of the day.
It was, in other words, just another night in the court of King Henry VIII.
Lesson nine.
Make yourself a family.
This is some more on Matthew.
My dad had all sorts of ideas about what family was, and none had to do with biology.
A family is a group of trusted associates.
More importantly, a family is a group of people who take each other seriously and who are
interested in one another's perspectives.
My father was always telling me that people were related to me.
He would introduce me to someone and give them the title of cousin.
The most honored title was uncle.
There are no women.
Matthew was one of my many uncles.
These terms were earned through merit and not blood.
One day, Matthew told my father that a young woman had moved in with him.
She was very beautiful, he said.
She kept him up all night wanting to dance in the kitchen and have drinks.
She wore a yellow dress, he said, and he loved it.
